summary:
Varun Shenoy, co-founder of Long Lake, opens by framing AI deployment as a diffusion problem: capabilities have arrived but real-world adoption lags, just as electricity took a generation to transform factories after Edison's Pearl Street demo. Long Lake raised over $3B and acquired 35 services businesses across HOA/property management, architecture, HR, and a $6.3B take-private of Amex Global Business Travel. Roughly 40% of staff focus on technology. Long Lake is the operator-owner, not a vendor, so AI failures are their own problem.

Shenoy maps agent maturity on a ladder: copilot → synchronous → asynchronous → long-running → AI coworker. Agents must earn each rung through in-field iteration. Engineers already parallelize work via async coding agents; the open frontier is replicating that async parallelism for serial services work. Representing knowledge work as code exploits strong coding capabilities while waiting for models to mature.

Real-world services tasks live off the internet but come with ground truth—did the roof get fixed? Human-agent collaboration produces rich traces (tool calls, hiccups) enabling auto-scored evals, OOD post-training data, and ratcheting weekly regression tests.

Finally, Shenoy argues continual learning and enablement are one loop: more usage drives continual learning, which improves the agent, which drives more usage. The elephant is first usage itself—100-year-old firms don't change on their own. His answer is extreme software-service co-design: embedding products natively into Excel, ERPs, Outlook, or 3D design software, and physically showing up—lunch-and-learns, trade-conference cotton-candy stands, mountain biking with operators. AI diffusion cannot be co-designed over Zoom; you have to touch grass.

sections.title: The diffusion framing and who Long Lake is
sections.summary: Opens with the demo-vs-deployment gap as the central question, uses electricity (1880s Pearl Street) to Ford's 1924 electrified assembly line to argue diffusion takes a generation, and positions AI diffusion as the defining problem for the next 20 years. Introduces Long Lake: $3B+ raised, 35 acquired services businesses across HOA/property management, architecture, HR, and a $6.3B take-private of Amex GBT. Roughly 40% of staff are on technology. Frames Long Lake as operator-owner, not vendor, so AI failures are their own problem.

sections.title: The copilot-to-coworker ladder and earning autonomy
sections.summary: Walks the autonomy spectrum—copilot → synchronous → asynchronous → long-running → AI coworker—and cautions against jumping to coworker. Argues agents must earn the right to more autonomy because models aren't ready for some tasks and field teams need to understand this is early-stage AI. Uses the jagged frontier: coding agents are mature, so synchronous and asynchronous coding flows are largely solved.

sections.title: Engineers parallelize, services don't
sections.summary: Highlights that engineers comfortably launch ten jobs and accept non-deterministic completion order—the async/forking pattern is natural for code. For services, the synchronous equivalent is a co-working agent with deep enterprise context, MCPs, and custom integrations. The open frontier is what async-for-services looks like, and how to parallelize traditionally serial work like clearing an inbox one email at a time. Poses three questions: represent knowledge work as code, parallelize serial work, find industry-specific async form factors.

sections.title: Real-world data, traces, and ground-truth evals
sections.summary: Argues the most valuable tasks—closing books with missing receipts, scoping buildings from blueprints, coordinating roof vendors—aren't online; they live in heads and 20-year-old software. Describes a flywheel where agents collaborate with employees, generating rich traces (tool calls, hiccups, papercuts). These enable automatically-scored ground-truth evals (did the roof actually get fixed?), which hill-climb better agents. Three upshots: automated evals with implicit + explicit feedback; out-of-distribution post-training data most labs lack; weekly hill-climbing benchmarks becoming regression tests. Continues into post-training discussion.

sections.title: Customization, the real shape of work, and continual learning as enablement
sections.summary: Long Lake post-trains its own models on proprietary data because frontier models can't yet do the work. Real-world tasks demand per-company, per-user, and per-client customization. Uses a hills-and-ravines vs. clear-slope metaphor: LLM tasks look like a clean slope, but actual work is full of exceptions that are the whole job. Argues continual learning and enablement—traditionally separate teams—form one loop: more usage drives continual learning, which improves the agent, which drives more usage. The remaining elephant is securing first usage.

sections.title: Extreme software-service co-design and the in-person imperative
sections.summary: Getting initial usage is the hardest problem; simply handing out Claude Code doesn't make 100-year-old firms change. Long Lake's answer is extreme software-service co-design, analogous to Jensen's extreme hardware-software co-design: products must be co-designed with the people and processes of acquired businesses, which is only possible from under the same roof. Means meeting users metaphorically—embedding natively into Excel, ERPs, 3D design software, Outlook/Gmail—and physically: lunch-and-learns, running cotton-candy stands at trade conferences, mountain biking with operators. Concludes that AI diffusion cannot be codesigned over Zoom; you have to touch grass.

organization.name: Long Lake
organization.summary: Long Lake (Long Lake Management) is an independent 2023 operator-owner founded by Alex Taubman and colleagues, including speaker Varun Shenoy. The official homepage states it applies frontier technology with management teams across the American services sector, with offices in New York, San Francisco, and Bloomfield Hills. First-party press and the May 4, 2026 SEC exhibit 99.1 describe a proprietary Nexus AI transformation platform used to accelerate acquired services businesses, and announce the $6.3 billion take-private of American Express Global Business Travel. Investors named on those pages include General Catalyst, Alpha Wave, Elad Gil, D1, Thrive, and Koch Equity Development. Media contact is media@llmh.com.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. Homepage is live. The Amex GBT transaction was announced May 4, 2026 and is expected to close in the second half of 2026, subject to stockholder and regulatory approvals. No ownership change of Long Lake itself since the August 28, 2026 talk.
